tiles.cap: The last ice on Puncak Jaya: 4.31 km² in 1988, 0.09 km² by 2025. Could be gone around 2030
tiles.nums: of the 1988 ice remained on Puncak Jaya by September 2025: about 0.09 km², down from 4.31 km²
tiles.p1: Puncak Jaya, in Indonesia’s Sudirman Range, still carries a few patches of ice, and NASA’s Earth Observatory has just put two Landsat images of them side by side, taken on 3 November 1988 and 19 October 2026. In 1988 the glaciers covered about 4.31 km². By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed only about 0.09 km² left, roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent. Recent satellite research suggests the main ice areas could disappear around 2030; BMKG’s own estimates say the ice could be gone much sooner.
tiles.p2: Why now: the images went up on Monday 16 November. An aerial survey planned for December should give an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, says Donaldi Permana of Indonesia’s meteorology, climatology and geophysics agency BMKG.
deep: Thinner every year
At one site, the East Northwall Firn, the ice went from 32 metres thick in 2010 to 4 metres in 2023. By November 2024 the ice at that site was gone.
El Niño years hit hardest

During the 2015–2016 El Niño the ice thinned about five times faster than usual, roughly 5.3 metres in a single year. The 2023–2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 metres a year.
Two satellites, 38 years apart
The 1988 image came from the Thematic Mapper on Landsat 5, the 2026 image from the Operational Land Imager on Landsat 9. Same mountain, 38 years on, and the white has almost gone.
The picture
A false-colour Landsat 9 view of the summit area on 19 October 2026. Credit NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya, 16 Nov 2026 (story Kathryn Hansen, images Lauren Dauphin)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin (Landsat 9)

tiles.cap: Tonight after sunset: point your phone at the sky and flash V-G-R at Voyager 1
tiles.nums: from Wednesday 18 November at 6:16 pm Singapore time, light leaving Earth takes a full day to reach Voyager 1, 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion km) away
tiles.p1: Tonight, Tuesday 17 November, after sunset, NASA is asking people everywhere to signal skyward for Voyager 1, in what it calls Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day. NASA’s Voyager site has an “Automated V-G-R Flasher” page: open it on a phone or tablet, point the screen at the sky, and it flashes V-G-R, Voyager’s call sign, in Morse code. Or do it by hand with a torch, bike light or glow stick: V is three quick flashes then one long, G is two long then one quick, R is quick, long, quick. A dot is under a second, a dash about a second, leave a second or more between letters, and keep going for about a minute.
tiles.p2: Why tomorrow: at 5:16:07 am US Eastern on Wednesday 18 November, 6:16 pm in Singapore, Voyager 1 will be 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 km) from Earth, the distance light travels in 24 hours. NASA says no other human-made object has reached that distance.
deep: How far a light-day is

NASA’s page lists the light-times for comparison: the Moon about 1.3 seconds away, the Sun about 8 minutes 20 seconds, Mars 3 to 22 minutes depending on where the two planets are, Neptune four hours and ten minutes, Proxima Centauri about 4.24 light-years. Voyager 1 left Earth on 5 September 1977; NASA’s page gives its speed as nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), though a caption on the same page says around 35,000 mph.
The code

V is · · · —, G is — — ·, R is · — ·. NASA’s timing: a dot under one second, a dash about one second, a brief pause between the symbols of a letter and a second or more between letters, repeated for about a minute. Any light does: torch, glow stick, solar lantern, bike light or phone.
Thursday’s panel

A panel at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Thursday 19 November at 12 pm US Eastern, Friday 20 November at 1 am in Singapore, can be watched online on NASA’s site; participants include Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, and Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager. NASA says a Voyager documentary is planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
The picture
An artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft, credit NASA/JPL-Caltech.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Voyager: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day (Stephen Carney) · Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day? (updated 12 Nov 2026) · NASA advisory M26-086, 10 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov

tiles.cap: Leonids before dawn tomorrow, up to 15 an hour after moonset. Mars and Jupiter drift apart
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors under ideal skies in the early hours of 18 November, after the Moon has set; most people will see fewer
tiles.p1: NASA’s skywatching notes for November put the Leonid meteor shower at its best in the early morning hours of Tuesday 17 and Wednesday 18 November, after the Moon sets: up to about 15 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, fewer for most viewers. Around 12 November the Northern Taurids peaked at a gentler 5 an hour. On the mornings of 15 and 16 November Mars and Jupiter stood about 1.2° apart in the south-east before sunrise; NASA says to keep watching on later mornings as they separate, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish beside it.
tiles.p2: Why now: New Moon was 8 November and first quarter is 17 November; NASA says to look after the Moon sets.
deep: Watch several mornings
NASA suggests watching Mars and Jupiter on more than one morning, to see them close in and then separate again. Jupiter is the brighter of the two.
Three supermoons
The full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon, the first of three in a row: November, December and January. Third quarter follows on 30 November.
Faced the right way

NASA’s chart for 17 November also marks where Voyager 1 sits, in Ophiuchus toward the western horizon at about 5 pm on 17 November, the evening NASA invites people to celebrate Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth.
The photo
NASA’s page opens with the full Moon rising over Vasquez Rocks, north of Los Angeles, photographed by Preston Dyches of NASA on 24 June 2021.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA (Raquel Villanueva), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: 241 days, 3,856 orbits: Expedition 74’s crews tell their story. Tomorrow, 8 am Singapore
tiles.nums: orbits of Earth by the Soyuz MS-28 crew in 241 days, more than 102 million miles, NASA says
tiles.p1: NASA welcomes the astronauts of Expedition 74 home at Space Center Houston on Tuesday 17 November at 6 pm Central time, which is Wednesday 18 November at 8 am in Singapore; the crew share mission highlights, followed by an awards ceremony. Chris Williams flew with Roscosmos’ Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev on Soyuz MS-28, launched from Baikonur on 27 November 2025 and landed in Kazakhstan on 26 July: 241 days, 3,856 orbits, more than 102 million miles. Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and ESA’s Sophie Adenot flew SpaceX Crew-12, launched 13 February and splashed down off Los Angeles on 8 October: 237 days, more than 3,792 orbits, more than 100 million miles.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Expedition 74 logged more than 1,400 hours of research, including 3D printing of metal and of tissue, blood-flow research and cancer-related pharmaceutical work.
deep: Who is on stage

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and Chris Williams; ESA’s Sophie Adenot; Roscosmos’ Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev. Andrey Fedyaev of Roscosmos, who flew on Crew-12, is not available.
Two ways up, two ways down

Soyuz MS-28 went up from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan and came down on land south-east of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. Crew-12 went up from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral and came down in the Pacific off Los Angeles.
The photo
The station over the Atlantic, photographed by ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot during the expedition.
tiles.src: NASA Johnson release J26-002, 10 Nov 2026: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston

tiles.cap: A star of 33+ Suns flares every 113 days. Chandra caught the hidden partner feeding on it
tiles.nums: between outbursts of AT 2016blu, a star at least 33 times the Sun’s mass in the galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years away
tiles.p1: For 15 years astronomers have watched a star called AT 2016blu, in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559 about 30 million light-years from Earth, brighten and dim on a schedule: at least 27 bursts of visible light between 2012 and 2026, roughly one every 113 days. The star is at least 33 times the mass of the Sun. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, pointed at it in March 2026, found it at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than in 2001–2002.
tiles.p2: Why now: the paper by Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia and colleagues appeared in The Astrophysical Journal on Monday 9 November; NASA ran the image as a picture feature on Friday 13 November.
deep: The hidden partner

The team’s explanation: a companion nobody can see directly, either a stellar-mass black hole or a neutron star, circles the big star on an oval orbit. Every 113 days, at closest approach, it pulls gas off the star.
X-rays first, then light

Gas falling onto the compact companion gets very hot and shines in X-rays. The team suspects those X-ray blasts heat the dense gas around the pair, which then glows in visible light, says co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona.
Who watched

The record of outbursts came from the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope, the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Supernova Project and more than 30 amateur astronomers of the AAVSO. “Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen,” says Aghakhanloo.
The picture

A composite of Chandra X-ray and Sloan Digital Sky Survey optical images of NGC 4559. Credit X-ray: NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al.; Optical: SDSS; Image Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/P. Edmonds.
tiles.src: NASA Chandra, NASA’s Chandra Finds Source of Star’s Mysterious Outbursts, 9 Nov 2026 (Megan Watzke) · NASA image article Outbursts from a Massive Star, 13 Nov 2026 · The Astrophysical Journal
tiles.credit: Image: NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al.; Optical: SDSS; Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/P. Edmonds

tiles.cap: IIT Madras trains self-steering ships inside a video-game engine, tuned to a 320 m tanker
tiles.nums: the length of the benchmark tanker used to calibrate SEANAV, IIT Madras’s digital twin of the maritime world, built on the Unity3D game engine
tiles.p1: SEANAV, from the Department of Ocean Engineering at IIT Madras, is a digital twin: a real-time copy of the sea in which an autonomous ship’s software can be tested and trained before it touches real water. It runs on Unity3D, the engine behind many video games, and was calibrated against a tanker about 320 metres long. Inside it the virtual ship reads simulated LiDAR, marine radar and stereo vision cameras, complete with the noise and delays real sensors have.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: shipping carries more than 80 percent of world trade. The team, led by Dr Suresh Rajendran, published the work in ASME’s Journal of Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering and announced it on Thursday 12 November.
deep: What the ship learned

In the simulator the vessel followed planned paths and used AI to avoid collisions under realistic waves and sensing. Several autonomous vessels can operate and learn together while obeying COLREGs, the international rules for avoiding collisions at sea.
Standing on the bridge

A VR interface on Meta Quest headsets puts a person on the virtual ship’s bridge. The work was presented at the ASME OMAE conferences in Vancouver in 2025 and Tokyo in 2026, and Dr Athira M. Nambiar of SRM Institute of Science and Technology headed the research with Rajendran.
Next: Indian ports

The team plans digital twins of major Indian ports, and says the platform could strengthen safety at ports such as Chennai, Mumbai, Visakhapatnam and Kochi; it also plans tests against physical scale models. “SEANAV provides a realistic and scalable platform for developing and validating autonomous maritime navigation technologies,” says Rajendran.
The picture
IIT Madras’s image for the SEANAV release, 12 November 2026. Credit IIT Madras.
tiles.src: IIT Madras press release, IIT Madras develops real-time digital twin platform for autonomous Maritime Navigation, 12 Nov 2026 · Journal of Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering (ASME)

tiles.cap: Shake a card of paper rings: the biggest dances first. Buildings aren’t equal in a quake
tiles.nums: the longest strip; each next one about 8 cm shorter, all 2.5 cm wide, taped into rings standing in a row on a 30 cm piece of cardboard
tiles.p1: Cut four or five paper strips 2.5 cm wide, the longest about 50 cm and each next one about 8 cm shorter. Tape each into a ring and tape the rings in a row on a piece of cardboard. Shake the card back and forth, starting slowly and speeding up: the biggest ring starts swinging first, then the next, and the smallest only when you shake fastest. Keep speeding up and the biggest ring comes alive again, in a new shape.
tiles.p2: Why: every ring has resonant frequencies set by its mass and its stiffness. “Stiffer objects have higher resonant frequencies, whereas more massive ones have lower resonant frequencies.”
deep: The biggest goes first

“The biggest ring has the largest mass and the least stiffness, so it has the lowest resonant frequency.” Slow shaking matches it; the small stiff ring needs fast shaking. Each ring has more than one resonant frequency, which is why the big one wakes again at a higher speed, in a different shape.
Earthquakes

“Here’s one reason not all buildings are equal in an earthquake.” Two buildings of different sizes may respond very differently to the ground’s vibrations, and how a building is built, its stiffness, matters as much as its size.
Hear the beat

Tape paper over both ends of a 2.5 cm piece of straw with a small BB pellet inside, tape it along the edge of the card, and the pellet taps out your shaking frequency. Shake up and down instead of side to side and the rings answer at different frequencies again.
Count it
Count your shakes per second when the biggest ring wakes, then when the smallest does. That ratio is a number nobody has measured for your rings.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks, Resonant Rings (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

tiles.cap: 17,000 t of argon at −185 °C, 1.5 km down, waiting for neutrinos fired from 1,300 km away
tiles.nums: from Fermilab in Batavia, Illinois, to the DUNE far detectors at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota
tiles.p1: Nearly 1.5 km underground in South Dakota, crews from Fermilab, CERN and the Sanford Underground Research Facility have begun building the first of two giant cryostats for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, CERN reported on Tuesday 10 November. Each is an insulated container 66 m long, 19 m wide and 18 m high that will hold about 17,000 tonnes of liquid argon at about −185 °C. The two cryostats together will use 2,600 red steel beams, part of more than 6,200 tonnes of steel contributed by CERN and carried one by one from the surface down to the assembly area. By 2031 a neutrino beam from Fermilab, 1,300 km away, is expected to reach it.
tiles.p2: Why: neutrinos may explain why the Universe ended up mostly matter; the detector will also watch particles arriving from the Sun and from deep space.
deep: Timeline

Assembly of the second cryostat starts in 2027 in the North Cavern; the underground space is to be completed by 2029, the detector by 2030, and the beam is expected by 2031. The experiment is slated to run until the late 2040s. More than 1,500 researchers are in the collaboration today, 1,800 from 2030.
Who said what

“DUNE is Fermilab’s top priority,” said Norbert Holtkamp, the director of Fermilab. “SURF is proud to support this world-class research 1478 metres below ground level,” said Mike Headley, the lab’s director. “This brings us one step closer to science,” said Jolie Macier, project manager for the far detectors and cryogenics.
CERN’s part

“Collaboration is in CERN’s DNA, and our contribution to DUNE is a brilliant example of cross-organisational partnership,” said Mark Thomson, CERN’s Director-General. The steel came from CERN as an in-kind contribution; Lluís Miralles, principal project engineer of CERN’s Neutrino Platform, is quoted on the build.
The picture
Construction of the cryostats began in early November, photographed by Matthew Kapust of SURF.
tiles.src: CERN, 10 Nov 2026: Construction begins on massive underground neutrino experiment designed to unlock the secrets of the Universe
tiles.credit: Photo: Matthew Kapust, SURF, via CERN

tiles.cap: A 6K gaming monitor: 21 million pixels at 165 Hz, or one button trades them for 330 Hz
tiles.nums: pixels per inch on Samsung’s 32-inch Odyssey G8 G80HS: 6144 × 3456 in 6K mode, or 3072 × 1728 at 330 Hz in its Dual Mode
tiles.p1: Samsung’s Odyssey G8 G80HS is a 32-inch flat IPS monitor with 6144 × 3456 pixels, about 21 million, refreshing 165 times a second. Press a button and it switches to 3072 × 1728 at 330 Hz: a quarter of the pixels, twice the frames, from the same panel driven two ways. It has a DisplayPort 2.1 input and two HDMI 2.1, claims 1 ms response, 350 cd/m² typical brightness and 400 peak, and costs $1,599.99.
tiles.p2: Why now: TIME put it on its Best Inventions of 2026 list on 15 October; Samsung calls it the industry’s first 6K gaming monitor.
deep: The engineering

An IPS panel with 1,000:1 contrast and 178° viewing angles, HDR10+ Gaming, 99% sRGB coverage, 7.4 kg with its stand, which lifts 120 mm, tilts, swivels ±30° and pivots ±92°. Maximum power draw 100 W from an external adapter.
What the reviewer measured

Tom’s Guide’s Tony Polanco measured 369.6 nits in SDR and 380 in HDR, 142.4% of the sRGB gamut, 100.9% of DCI-P3 and a colour error (Delta-E) of 0.24. An OLED rival he had tested, the Asus ROG Swift OLED PG34WCDN, reached 200.7% sRGB and 142.2% DCI-P3.
What was wrong

“Pricey.” Hues “slightly oversaturated” in sRGB and colours not as vivid as OLED rivals: “We wish it had an OLED panel and cost a bit less.” No speakers, ports “nearly impossible to connect and disconnect” by touch, and in Cyberpunk 2077 his powerful PC “wasn’t quite able to hit 165 frames per second”.
Do the sums
6144 × 3456 = 21,233,664 pixels, each redrawn 165 times a second: about 3.5 billion pixel updates every second.
tiles.src: Samsung spec sheets (Canada, US), Odyssey G8 G80HS (LS32HG802ESXZA) · TIME Best Inventions 2026, 15 Oct 2026 (Chris Stokel-Walker) · Tom’s Guide review, 29 Aug 2026 (Tony Polanco)

tiles.cap: DJI’s Osmo 360 II: every direction in 8K, 60 frames a second. Overheated after 45 minutes
tiles.nums: 7680 × 3840 pixels, 60 frames a second, from two square sensors, each with a 360° imaging area equivalent to a 1-inch 4:3 sensor; 183 g
tiles.p1: Two lenses back to back, each on a square image sensor with 2.4 μm pixels, record the whole sphere around the camera at 7680 × 3840 and 60 frames a second, in 10-bit colour with 14.5 stops of dynamic range. DJI says the square sensor keeps the same 360° image field as a traditional 1-inch rectangular sensor while using 25 percent more of the sensor’s area. 183 g, 105 GB of storage built in, waterproof to 10 m, and lenses you can swap.
tiles.p2: Why now: Tom’s Guide’s Peter Wolinski published his review on Friday 13 November and called it the first and, so far, the only 360 camera to shoot 8K at 60 fps.
deep: The battery test

DJI claims up to 100 minutes of 8K/30. In the reviewer’s standard indoor test it managed 88. At 8K/60 it overheated after 45 minutes, then recorded about 21 more with the screen disabled: 66 in all. The 2,150 mAh battery charges to 80 percent in 22 minutes.
What else was wrong

“Very expensive in the US” at $699, and “Wind reduction nothing special”: the microphones clipped on the loud noise of an engine. Insta360’s app, he found, is still the easiest for a straight-to-social workflow, and reframing clips is clunkier in DJI’s Mimo app.
Same sensors, new brain

The two 1/1.1-inch square sensors are the ones in the 2025 Osmo 360; the jump to 8K/60 comes from new image processing. Stitching “wasn’t noticeable, even at ultra-wide FoVs”; the only artefact is the dead spot where the selfie stick sits.
Numbers
120-megapixel 360° photos, 16K 360° timelapses, slow motion to 8K/120, works at −20 °C, €599 for the standard combo in Europe.
tiles.src: DJI press release, 3 Sep 2026 · DJI Store spec sheet, Osmo 360 II · Tom’s Guide review, 13 Nov 2026 (Peter Wolinski)

tiles.cap: Northeast Monsoon setting in: 32–34 °C, afternoon storms. Paya Lebar hit 35.4 °C on 4 Nov
tiles.nums: of rain fell around Rivervale Drive on 6 November, the biggest daily total of the first half of the month
tiles.p1: NEA’s outlook for the rest of November, issued Monday 16 November, says Northeast Monsoon conditions are expected to set in over Singapore in the second half of the month as the prevailing winds strengthen and shift to blow from the northeast or northwest. Expect short thundery showers over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days, running into the night on a few days; on some days the showers could be widespread and heavy. Daily highs of 32 to 34 °C, slightly above 34 on a few days; around 23 °C on some rainy days.
tiles.p2: Looking back at 1–15 November: 35.4 °C at Paya Lebar on 4 November, the month’s high so far, and daily maxima above 34 °C on seven occasions.
deep: Uneven rain

About half the island had above-average rain in the first half of November. Somerset was 44 percent above its average; Tanjong Katong 65 percent below. Total rainfall for the second half is forecast to be slightly above the long-term average over most of the island.
6 November
Widespread moderate to heavy thundery showers; 94.2 mm around Rivervale Drive that day, the highest daily total of the fortnight.
Haze: over

NEA’s final haze update of the season was on 7 November, when the 24-hour PSI was 51–55, moderate. On 16 November its regional page reported showers over much of the ASEAN region and only few to isolated hotspots.
The picture
The image from NEA’s outlook page of 16 November 2026. Credit NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore.
tiles.src: NEA / Meteorological Service Singapore, Wet Weather To Continue For Rest Of November 2026 With Onset Of Northeast Monsoon, 16 Nov 2026 · NEA haze situation update, 7 Nov 2026 · NEA regional haze situation, 16 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: NTU and Canaan put S$7 million into AI that runs on less power, out at the edge
tiles.nums: over four years for the NTU–Canaan Green Intelligent Compute Collaboration, announced Friday 13 November: four PhD researchers, about 10 papers, four technical reports and working prototypes
tiles.p1: AI is moving out of giant data centres and into retail, cameras and devices at the “edge”, and every one of them uses electricity. In a release on Friday 13 November, NTU and Canaan said they have launched a four-year, S$7 million collaboration, hosted at NTU’s Centre in Computational Technologies for Finance, to design energy-aware computing, privacy-preserving edge AI for smart retail, inference shared between cloud, edge and end devices, and new edge-AI training modules. It is to produce four PhD researchers, about 10 academic papers, four technical work-package reports, industrial prototypes and patents where commercially applicable.
tiles.p2: Why here: NTU ties the work to Singapore’s updated National AI Strategy (2026), its Green Data Centre Roadmap and the Singapore Standard SS 715:2025.
deep: The problem

“As AI moves beyond centralised data centres and into more diverse real-world environments, computing efficiency is becoming a system-level challenge - spanning chips, software, workload scheduling and energy use,” said Nangeng Zhang, Canaan’s founder, chairman and CEO.
NTU’s view

“As artificial intelligence expands across every sector, managing its environmental footprint has become a critical global challenge,” said Professor Shirley Meng, NTU’s Vice President (Industry). The agreement was first signed on 7 May 2026; the research team is led by Associate Professor Tianwei Zhang, Associate Director of the centre and Provost’s Chair in computing.
The photo
Representatives from NTU and Canaan at the launch, among them Nangeng Zhang, Professor Shirley Meng and Professor Wen Yonggang, NTU’s Vice Provost (Graduate Education) and Director of the centre.
tiles.src: NTU News, 13 Nov 2026: S$7 million NTU-Canaan partnership to drive advances in sustainable computing and edge AI · NTU CCTF news, 7 May 2026

tiles.cap: A metre of string across your ears: pluck it and you hear a note nobody else can
tiles.nums: the pitch of a string rises with the square root of its tension, and rises as the string gets shorter; the sound is so quiet that nobody close to you is disturbed
tiles.p1: Take a piece of string at least 1 m long. Put the middle behind your head, bring the two halves forward across your ears so the string crosses each ear opening, and hold the loose ends together in front of your face. Pluck. You hear your string, but so quietly that, the Exploratorium says, you will not disturb other people even if they are close to you. Pull tighter: the note goes up. Slide your hand along to shorten the string while keeping the pull the same: higher again.
tiles.p2: The rule, from the Exploratorium: frequency is proportional to the square root of the tension and inversely proportional to the length; higher frequency is a higher note.
deep: Two knobs

Tension and length are the two things you can change. Double the tension and the frequency rises by √2, about 1.41 times; halve the length at the same tension and it doubles. Try to hear the difference between the two moves.
Why only you
The Exploratorium does not say why the sound stays with you; ask a friend to stand a hand’s width away and report what they hear, then swap places.
The Exploratorium’s joke
“Many city bus services do not allow people to play loud music on buses,” the Exploratorium notes; a head harp keeps you within the rules, and you get “more room as others move away from you.”

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at the University of Pennsylvania put it in six words. Do not hand over the things you enjoy and that give you meaning, he says, and decide which skills you want to protect. Trent Cash, a behavioural scientist at the University of Waterloo, adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient, and he does not think AI is going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. Back on their own, they did not detect the growths as well.
The readers who gave up

People who used an AI tool to solve SAT questions were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because persistence is key for learning.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, “Is AI making us dumber? Depends how it’s used”, Meghan Rosen, 13 Oct 2026 · Cash et al., Trends in Cognitive Sciences, Aug 2026 · Lira et al., arXiv preprint, Feb 2026

tiles.cap: Five ocean layers: sunlight ends at 200 m; the abyssal zone runs from 4,000 to 6,000 m down
tiles.nums: almost: the depth of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific, some 2,550 km long and about 70 km wide on average
tiles.p1: Scientists describe the ocean’s depths in five layers. The sunlight zone ends at 200 metres. The midnight zone begins at 1,000 metres. Below that comes the abyssal zone, beginning at 4,000 metres by NOAA’s definition, though other experts say 2,000; everyone agrees it extends down to 6,000 metres. No sunlight reaches it, and the only light there comes from life forms. Below it lies the hadal zone: the Mariana Trench descends to almost 11,000 metres.
tiles.p2: Why now: Science News Explores published this on Monday 16 November, noting that in 2026 scientists found glowing giant sea spiders in the abyssal zone.
deep: The trench

The Mariana Trench, in the western Pacific Ocean, descends to almost 11,000 metres. It is some 2,550 km long and about 70 km wide on average, and marks where two of Earth’s tectonic plates are colliding, forcing one to dive beneath the other.
Light from life
“The only light there comes from life forms.” Among them, in 2026, glowing giant sea spiders found in the abyssal zone.
Stack the numbers
200, 1,000, 4,000, 6,000, 11,000 metres. Each step down is a different world, and only the top one ever sees the Sun.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, Scientists Say: Abyssal Zone, 16 Nov 2026 (Katie Grace Carpenter)

tiles.cap: October 2026 ran 1.43 °C above the 20th-century average, the most of any month since 1850
tiles.nums: Octobers in a row warmer than the 20th-century average; all 10 of the warmest Octobers on record have come since 2015
tiles.p1: NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information published its October report on 12 November. The global surface temperature was 1.43 °C (2.57 °F) above the 20th-century average, the highest departure for any month in the 1850–2026 record: 0.08 °C above the previous October record, set in 2023, and 0.03 °C above the previous record for any month, shared by September and November 2023. The ocean surface was 1.14 °C above average, the highest for any month on record and the fifth monthly record in a row; land was 2.08 °C above, third highest for an October.
tiles.p2: Why here: Asia had its second-warmest October on record. January to October 2026 was the second warmest such period, behind 2024, and NCEI says 2026 will very likely finish among the five warmest years.
deep: Storms

Fifteen tropical storms formed worldwide in October; 12 reached tropical cyclone strength and 11 reached major intensity, both all-time records for the month. The eastern North Pacific had six, tying its October record from 1992 and 2018; the Atlantic had only two, and Hurricane Isaias was the latest first hurricane of any Atlantic season in the satellite era.
Ice and snow

Global sea ice was the third smallest for October in 48 years of records: 8.89 million square miles, 1.04 million below the 1991–2020 average. The Antarctic was 730,000 square miles below average, its second-smallest October. Northern Hemisphere snow cover, 7.07 million square miles, was below average; Eurasia had its smallest October snow cover since 2011.
Why a “departure”

Climate scientists compare each month with the same month’s long-term average, so that a hot October and a hot January can be set side by side. A departure of 1.43 °C for a whole planet, for a whole month, is the biggest in 177 years of records.
tiles.src: NOAA NCEI, Monitoring Global Temperature and Precipitation in October 2026, 12 Nov 2026
